subcomponents.title: Scaffold detection, location, dependencies, and style neutrality

criteria.rationale: Every clause is met. (1) What SKILL.md directs: SKILL.md:11-14 resolves template paths from SKILL_DIR. SKILL.md:37-66 names the three anchors and resolves an empty or standalone project to its root. When no anchor is present it copies all of SKILL_DIR/templates/bootstrap/. It merges the full dependency set, says "Do not assume anything is already installed", runs npm ci or npm install, then runs `npx playwright install chromium` if Chromium is missing. That is an install guarded by an availability check, not just a sentence saying Chromium is required. (2) What the template contains: package.json has react, react-dom, motion, lucide-react, vite, @vitejs/plugin-react, typescript, the eslint stack, playwright and vitest, with build, verify and inspect scripts. vite.config.ts is the Vite + React build setup. src/presentations/index.ts is the registry that maps a slug to a lazily loaded route component. subcomponents.title: Verification tooling robustness

criteria.rationale: Both copies of preview.mjs (repository and bootstrap template) have the same startPreview. It spawns `process.execPath` running vite's own bin/vite.js with `preview`, so the tracked child is the preview server itself rather than an npm or npx wrapper. Its stop() sends SIGTERM and waits for the child's 'exit' event, up to 3 seconds. If the child is still running, stop() sends SIGKILL and waits again. stop() is idempotent. If readiness fails, startPreview calls stop() before it throws. In verify.mjs renderPhase (both copies), startPreview and launchChromium both run inside a try whose finally does `await browser?.close()` and then `await preview?.stop()`. So success, a failing check (PhaseError thrown), a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through an awaited stop() of the server process. In inspect-presentation.mjs (both copies), startPreview runs just before a try that starts with launchChromium(). That try's finally closes the browser and runs `await preview.stop()`, which covers the same exit paths. Panels A and B match the source, and I adopt their pass verdict. Panel C is accurate that onSignal sends SIGKILL and then calls process.exit(130) without waiting for the child to exit. That does not decide the requirement. The paths the requirement and review guidance name are success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and an error after the preview started. All of these await stop(). An external SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP sent to the script is not one of those named paths. Even on that path, the handler sends SIGKILL to the server process itself, which the server cannot catch, so the server is still terminated. criteria.rationale: I rule with Judge C. The record leaves a substantial share of behavior unexercised that the environment did allow, and most of those gaps were the candidate's own choice. (1) Motion across steps was never observed. 'Stable entities morph across steps' (persisting entity morphs, new entity enters after others settle, departing entity exits) and 'Persistent grouped scenes' (grouped steps update in place, continuing entities are not faded as newcomers) are motion and timing behaviors. The log's 'entry/exit' evidence is only settled first, dense, sixth and final states plus helper screenshots, so it shows the scene accumulating, not how entities move. The criterion names this exact case (DOM persistence instead of motion sequencing) as a weaker property that does not cover the scenario. The browser could observe mid-transition: the ledger's U1 recorded sampled positions during a mode toggle. So this gap is not environmental, and the acceptance log never discloses it. (2) The verifier's failure paths were explicitly skipped: 'Missing sample fails', 'Console or page error fails verification', 'Step error fails verification', and the clear pass/fail outcome. The stated reason is that these cases belong to E2E-002, which is a choice to defer to automated tests, not an environmental limit. The same pass ran `npm run build` and `npm run inspect`. (3) The style-ownership scenarios (kit primitives expose style hooks, unstyled kit output, optional styling frameworks) were also left to repository tests. Judges A and B are right that the exercised navigation, mode, clamp, fit and inspection coverage is real, and that the skill-journey gaps are disclosed as environmental. But that does not decide the requirement. Judge A does not account for motion sequencing being observed only through settled states. Judge B points to U10 in the ledger as disclosure, but U10 describes the implementer's own verifier scope ('Motion: it was verified statically only'), not the acceptance pass's coverage. Even read as disclosure, the omission was chosen rather than environmental, so it still counts against coverage. Together, these chosen and undisclosed omissions leave a substantial share of the scene runtime's core behavior and of render verification unexercised.

presentation-skill.rationale: Every clause is met. (1) What SKILL.md directs: SKILL.md:11-14 resolves template paths from SKILL_DIR. SKILL.md:37-66 names the three anchors and resolves an empty or standalone project to its root. When no anchor is present it copies all of SKILL_DIR/templates/bootstrap/. It merges the full dependency set, says "Do not assume anything is already installed", runs npm ci or npm install, then runs `npx playwright install chromium` if Chromium is missing. That is an install guarded by an availability check, not just a sentence saying Chromium is required. (2) What the template contains: package.json has react, react-dom, motion, lucide-react, vite, @vitejs/plugin-react, typescript, the eslint stack, playwright and vitest, with build, verify and inspect scripts. vite.config.ts is the Vite + React build setup. src/presentations/index.ts is the registry that maps a slug to a lazily loaded route component. The scene kit is present in full: - types.ts holds the Step/Scene contract. - Stage.tsx is the host. It mounts the active step's Scene inside LayoutGroup/AnimatePresence, which runs the layoutId morphs, on the fit-scaled DESIGN_W×DESIGN_H canvas. - Presentation.tsx wires usePresentationNav (present/browse), the Header, Toc and Footer chrome (captions and ToC), and useFitScale. - index.ts exports all of them. (3) Alignment with the canonical kit: scripts/sync-templates.mjs findDrift byte-compares every non-test file under src/presentation-kit and scripts/lib, plus verify.mjs and inspect-presentation.mjs, against the bootstrap copies. It reports any differing, missing or extra file. template-drift.test.mjs and INT-001 both assert `findDrift(...)` equals []. Byte equality rules out any difference in behavior or public types, so line counts are not needed. (4) Materialization test: e2e/bootstrap.e2e.test.ts INT-001 runs mkdtempSync in tmpdir and cpSync's templatesDir('bootstrap') into outside/app. It asserts the dependency set and the three anchors, then runs npm ci, npm run build, npm run lint and npm run verify in that fresh directory, expecting exit code 0 and 'VERIFY PASS'. SKILL.md:55-57 has the starter removed once the first real presentation is registered. So it is presentation-owned styling, not a scaffold default. It also does not touch any clause of this criterion's scenario: full scaffold, anchors, dependency install, materialization test, or kit alignment.

result.rationale: The review guidance requires that the verifier never treat a missing or non-numeric data-step-index as progress. It says to fail when the check "converts an absent or non-numeric hook into a number that still satisfies its comparison (for example Number(null) === 0 on the first step)". In scripts/verify.mjs, renderPhase rejects only a null index (line 153). It then compares `Number(idx) !== i` (line 157). An empty or whitespace-only data-step-index is non-numeric, but Number('') and Number(' ') both evaluate to 0. That satisfies the comparison when i === 0, so the first step is accepted as valid without a numeric index hook. This is the coercion failure the guidance names, and it is what Judge B identified, so B's fail verdict is the one I rule. Judge A is right that a null index throws, that NaN fails the check, and that the count check rejects 0, NaN and null. Judge C is right that the waitForFunction transition check after ArrowRight is a strict string comparison. Neither point covers line 157, which coerces the index with Number() on every step, including step 0. So neither establishes that non-numeric hooks are always rejected. Both also cite the 'a transition does not advance' e2e fault, which does exist and asserts a non-zero exit at step index 3. That test covers the non-advancing transition, but it does not cure the coercion gap the guidance treats as a separate fail condition.

checks.rationale: The dissent's fact is accurate: in both copies of preview.mjs, onSignal calls onExit, which sends child.kill('SIGKILL'), and then calls process.exit(130) without waiting for the child's exit event. That fact does not decide the requirement. The requirement and its review guidance name four exit paths: success, a failing check, a browser launch failure, and an error thrown after the preview started. An external signal sent to the script is not one of them. In verify.mjs, renderPhase calls startPreview and launchChromium inside a try. Its finally closes the browser and runs `await preview?.stop()`. In inspect-presentation.mjs, launchChromium is the first call inside a try whose finally runs `await preview.stop()`. stop() sends SIGTERM and awaits the child's 'exit' event. If the child is still running after 3 seconds, it sends SIGKILL and awaits exit again. The child is the preview server itself, because the script spawns process.execPath on vite's bin/vite.js rather than an npm or npx wrapper. So every named path terminates the server and awaits its exit. engineering-quality.rationale: I traced every materialized template against its documented destination, the bootstrap layout and the kit types. All relative imports, the CSS import, required props and field names resolve. No focused materialize-and-build test exists, so the verdict rests on tracing. Destinations: SKILL.md and templates/presentation/README.md place presentation templates in <target>/src/presentations/<slug>/ (Scene.tsx.tmpl becomes TalkScene.tsx; step files go in steps/). templates/README.md places the bootstrap's scripts/** in <target>/scripts/. Imports: Talk.tsx.tmpl and Scene.tsx.tmpl import '../../presentation-kit', which resolves to src/presentation-kit from src/presentations/<slug>/. step.tsx.tmpl imports '../../../presentation-kit' from steps/, which also resolves to src/presentation-kit, so nothing escapes src. Its '../outline' and '../TalkScene' point at sibling outputs, and TalkScene exports TalkPayload. steps/index.ts.tmpl imports ./step1 and ./step2, the step instances. Talk.tsx.tmpl imports ./talk.css, ./outline and ./steps, all produced by the templates, and talk.css.tmpl has no @import. entities.ts.tmpl and outline.ts.tmpl have no imports. Kit exports: presentation-kit/index.ts exports Presentation, Box, Arrow, Appear, SceneLayer and the SceneProps and Step types. Required props: Presentation needs steps and title, and Talk.tsx.tmpl passes both (initialMode 'browse' is a valid Mode). Box needs id, passed as E.idea and E.detail. Arrow needs id, from and to, all passed. Appear and SceneLayer have no required props. Step<TalkPayload> needs id, era, title, caption and Scene; the step template spreads OUTLINE[__I__], whose entries carry id, era, title and caption, and sets Scene, groupKey and payload (both optional in types.ts). Type-check flags: tsconfig.app.json includes src and sets noUnusedLocals, verbatimModuleSyntax and erasableSyntaxOnly. The templates satisfy them: every import is used (Appear, Arrow, Box, SceneLayer, E, at), and type-only imports use import type. The bootstrap starter files are the same templates with tokens substituted, for example TalkScene.tsx with st- prefixes in place of __PREFIX__-. Inspect template: the bootstrap scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs imports ./lib/diagnostics.mjs and ./lib/preview.mjs, both shipped in bootstrap/scripts/lib, and package.json defines the inspect script as node scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs, so it resolves at its destination.

result.rationale: I rule with Judge C. The record leaves a substantial share of behavior unexercised that the environment did allow, and most of those gaps were the candidate's own choice. (1) Motion across steps was never observed. 'Stable entities morph across steps' (persisting entity morphs, new entity enters after others settle, departing entity exits) and 'Persistent grouped scenes' (grouped steps update in place, continuing entities are not faded as newcomers) are motion and timing behaviors. The log's 'entry/exit' evidence is only settled first, dense, sixth and final states plus helper screenshots, so it shows the scene accumulating, not how entities move. The criterion names this exact case (DOM persistence instead of motion sequencing) as a weaker property that does not cover the scenario. The browser could observe mid-transition: the ledger's U1 recorded sampled positions during a mode toggle. So this gap is not environmental, and the acceptance log never discloses it. (2) The verifier's failure paths were explicitly skipped: 'Missing sample fails', 'Console or page error fails verification', 'Step error fails verification', and the clear pass/fail outcome. The stated reason is that these cases belong to E2E-002, which is a choice to defer to automated tests, not an environmental limit. The same pass ran `npm run build` and `npm run inspect`. (3) The style-ownership scenarios (kit primitives expose style hooks, unstyled kit output, optional styling frameworks) were also left to repository tests. Judges A and B are right that the exercised navigation, mode, clamp, fit and inspection coverage is real, and that the skill-journey gaps are disclosed as environmental. But that does not decide the requirement. Judge A does not account for motion sequencing being observed only through settled states. Judge B points to U10 in the ledger as disclosure, but U10 describes the implementer's own verifier scope ('Motion: it was verified statically only'), not the acceptance pass's coverage. Even read as disclosure, the omission was chosen rather than environmental, so it still counts against coverage. Together, these chosen and undisclosed omissions leave a substantial share of the scene runtime's core behavior and of render verification unexercised.

testing-evidence.rationale: I rule with Judge C. The record leaves a substantial share of behavior unexercised that the environment did allow, and most of those gaps were the candidate's own choice. (1) Motion across steps was never observed. 'Stable entities morph across steps' (persisting entity morphs, new entity enters after others settle, departing entity exits) and 'Persistent grouped scenes' (grouped steps update in place, continuing entities are not faded as newcomers) are motion and timing behaviors. The log's 'entry/exit' evidence is only settled first, dense, sixth and final states plus helper screenshots, so it shows the scene accumulating, not how entities move. The criterion names this exact case (DOM persistence instead of motion sequencing) as a weaker property that does not cover the scenario. The browser could observe mid-transition: the ledger's U1 recorded sampled positions during a mode toggle. So this gap is not environmental, and the acceptance log never discloses it. (2) The verifier's failure paths were explicitly skipped: 'Missing sample fails', 'Console or page error fails verification', 'Step error fails verification', and the clear pass/fail outcome. The stated reason is that these cases belong to E2E-002, which is a choice to defer to automated tests, not an environmental limit. The same pass ran `npm run build` and `npm run inspect`. (3) The style-ownership scenarios (kit primitives expose style hooks, unstyled kit output, optional styling frameworks) were also left to repository tests. Judges A and B are right that the exercised navigation, mode, clamp, fit and inspection coverage is real, and that the skill-journey gaps are disclosed as environmental. But that does not decide the requirement. Judge A does not account for motion sequencing being observed only through settled states. Judge B points to U10 in the ledger as disclosure, but U10 describes the implementer's own verifier scope ('Motion: it was verified statically only'), not the acceptance pass's coverage. Even read as disclosure, the omission was chosen rather than environmental, so it still counts against coverage. Together, these chosen and undisclosed omissions leave a substantial share of the scene runtime's core behavior and of render verification unexercised.

votes.rationale: Readiness is taken from HTTP polling of the port, not from the spawned child's own announcement. The child's exit is only sampled before each fetch, and the child is not raced against the poll. The port is also overridable by a fixed PREVIEW_PORT. A stale server already listening on the port could answer the poll before the child's exit is observed. A strict port alone is not sufficient.
evidence: startPreview picks the port with `port ?? (Number(process.env.PREVIEW_PORT) || (await freePort()))`, so a fixed or reused port is allowed.
freePort closes its server before the port is handed to vite, so the verifier does not hold the port.

first_results.rationale: The review guidance requires that the verifier never treat a missing or non-numeric data-step-index as progress. It says to fail when the check "converts an absent or non-numeric hook into a number that still satisfies its comparison (for example Number(null) === 0 on the first step)". In scripts/verify.mjs, renderPhase rejects only a null index (line 153). It then compares `Number(idx) !== i` (line 157). An empty or whitespace-only data-step-index is non-numeric, but Number('') and Number(' ') both evaluate to 0. That satisfies the comparison when i === 0, so the first step is accepted as valid without a numeric index hook. This is the coercion failure the guidance names, and it is what Judge B identified, so B's fail verdict is the one I rule. Judge A is right that a null index throws, that NaN fails the check, and that the count check rejects 0, NaN and null. Judge C is right that the waitForFunction transition check after ArrowRight is a strict string comparison. Neither point covers line 157, which coerces the index with Number() on every step, including step 0. So neither establishes that non-numeric hooks are always rejected. Both also cite the 'a transition does not advance' e2e fault, which does exist and asserts a non-zero exit at step index 3. That test covers the non-advancing transition, but it does not cure the coercion gap the guidance treats as a separate fail condition.

audit_results.rationale: The quoted lines show that one clause of the review guidance is unmet. The guidance says the verifier must not treat a missing or non-numeric data-step-index as progress. It says to fail when the check "converts an absent or non-numeric hook into a number that still satisfies its comparison (for example Number(null) === 0 on the first step)" and to cite the comparison. In scripts/verify.mjs, line 153 rejects only a null index. Line 157 then compares with `Number(idx) !== i`. An empty or whitespace-only data-step-index is not numeric, but Number('') and Number(' ') both evaluate to 0. On the first step (i === 0) that passes the comparison, so the verifier accepts step 0 with no numeric index hook. This is the first-step coercion the guidance names, so it is not a made-up scenario. Two other checks do not close this gap. The waitForFunction transition check on lines 172-176 compares strings strictly, but it only covers the index after ArrowRight. The count check on lines 145-147 rejects 0, NaN and null counts, but it does not cover the index. The claim names the unmet clause and cites the comparison that breaks it.

first_results.rationale: Both copies of preview.mjs (repository and bootstrap template) have the same startPreview. It spawns `process.execPath` running vite's own bin/vite.js with `preview`, so the tracked child is the preview server itself rather than an npm or npx wrapper. Its stop() sends SIGTERM and waits for the child's 'exit' event, up to 3 seconds. If the child is still running, stop() sends SIGKILL and waits again. stop() is idempotent. If readiness fails, startPreview calls stop() before it throws. In verify.mjs renderPhase (both copies), startPreview and launchChromium both run inside a try whose finally does `await browser?.close()` and then `await preview?.stop()`. So success, a failing check (PhaseError thrown), a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through an awaited stop() of the server process. In inspect-presentation.mjs (both copies), startPreview runs just before a try that starts with launchChromium(). That try's finally closes the browser and runs `await preview.stop()`, which covers the same exit paths. Panels A and B match the source, and I adopt their pass verdict. Panel C is accurate that onSignal sends SIGKILL and then calls process.exit(130) without waiting for the child to exit. That does not decide the requirement. The paths the requirement and review guidance name are success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and an error after the preview started. All of these await stop(). An external SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP sent to the script is not one of those named paths. Even on that path, the handler sends SIGKILL to the server process itself, which the server cannot catch, so the server is still terminated. This is not the failure the criterion describes, where only a wrapper is killed and the server it spawned keeps running.

audit_results.rationale: The quoted lines show the requirement is met in all four copies: the repository verify and inspect scripts, the template verify and inspect scripts, and both copies of the shared preview.mjs helper they use. 1. The tracked child is the preview server itself. startPreview spawns `process.execPath` running vite's own bin/vite.js with `preview`. It is not an npm or npx wrapper. 2. stop() terminates the server and waits for it to exit. It sends SIGTERM and waits for the child's 'exit' event, up to 3 seconds. If the child is still running, it sends SIGKILL and waits again. 3. A readiness failure stops the server. When the child exits early or the 30-second deadline passes, startPreview calls `await stop()` before it throws. 4. In both verify.mjs copies, startPreview and launchChromium run inside a try. Its finally runs `await browser?.close()` and then `await preview?.stop()`. Success, a failing check that throws PhaseError, a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through that finally. 5. In both inspect-presentation.mjs copies, startPreview runs just before the try. Nothing between them can throw. launchChromium is the first statement inside the try, and the finally runs `await preview.stop()`. Every exit path after the preview starts therefore stops it. The signal handler kills the server with SIGKILL without waiting before process.exit. An externally signalled script is not one of the exit paths the guidance names, and the server is still killed. Every path the requirement names is backed by quoted source.

first_results.rationale: I rule with Judge C. The record leaves a substantial share of behavior unexercised that the environment did allow, and most of those gaps were the candidate's own choice. (1) Motion across steps was never observed. 'Stable entities morph across steps' (persisting entity morphs, new entity enters after others settle, departing entity exits) and 'Persistent grouped scenes' (grouped steps update in place, continuing entities are not faded as newcomers) are motion and timing behaviors. The log's 'entry/exit' evidence is only settled first, dense, sixth and final states plus helper screenshots, so it shows the scene accumulating, not how entities move. The criterion names this exact case (DOM persistence instead of motion sequencing) as a weaker property that does not cover the scenario. The browser could observe mid-transition: the ledger's U1 recorded sampled positions during a mode toggle. So this gap is not environmental, and the acceptance log never discloses it. (2) The verifier's failure paths were explicitly skipped: 'Missing sample fails', 'Console or page error fails verification', 'Step error fails verification', and the clear pass/fail outcome. The stated reason is that these cases belong to E2E-002, which is a choice to defer to automated tests, not an environmental limit. The same pass ran `npm run build` and `npm run inspect`. (3) The style-ownership scenarios (kit primitives expose style hooks, unstyled kit output, optional styling frameworks) were also left to repository tests. Judges A and B are right that the exercised navigation, mode, clamp, fit and inspection coverage is real, and that the skill-journey gaps are disclosed as environmental. But that does not decide the requirement. Judge A does not account for motion sequencing being observed only through settled states. Judge B points to U10 in the ledger as disclosure, but U10 describes the implementer's own verifier scope ('Motion: it was verified statically only'), not the acceptance pass's coverage. Even read as disclosure, the omission was chosen rather than environmental, so it still counts against coverage. Together, these chosen and undisclosed omissions leave a substantial share of the scene runtime's core behavior and of render verification unexercised.

lines.text: - **Sample route, all nine step states, captions, entry/exit, and accumulating diagram:** Opened the registered route in AXI, inspected the first, dense third, sixth, and final states, and used the project-local helper to capture all nine step indices in order. The scene visibly accumulates the skill, card row, connectors, verification node, edit arc, and reveal frame. Footer title/caption and controls update by step; attribution link is present. The helper manifest records indices 0–8.

- **Keyboard navigation and endpoints:** ArrowRight advanced step 1→2. Clicking step 1 and pressing ArrowLeft stayed at 1, and clicking step 9 then pressing ArrowRight stayed at 9. At the final step, Next was disabled.

- **Direct jump / table of contents:** Clicking “The Gathering” jumped from step 2 to the first step in that era (step 3). Active step hooks and semantic current-step state were present in the DOM (`data-presentation-active="true"`, `aria-current="step"`).

- **Modes / position:** Pressing `p` while the mode toggle was focused did not also advance the step; the mode toggle itself changed present/browse mode while retaining index 2. Browse mode showed caption, ToC at desktop, progress and navigation; present mode hid those and retained title/marker. Attribution remained visible and linked.

- **Fixed canvas and composition:** AXI and helper screenshots were captured at 1440×900 and 390×844. The layout scales without internal reflow. At narrow width the diagram is too small to read (F-002). At desktop the step-card tray frame contradicts the explicit “tray is not framed” direction (F-001). engineering-quality.rationale: The readiness wait in startPreview is a polling loop bounded by a 30-second deadline: once it passes, the loop stops the preview and throws. It also exits when the child process exits. That satisfies 'every wait for preview readiness has a timeout.' The auditor's point is that one fetch has no per-request timeout and could, in principle, hang past the deadline. That only happens if the local preview server accepts a connection and never answers, which is a hypothetical the cited source does not produce and the guidance does not name. The guidance asks only whether a readiness wait lacks a timeout, and this one has one. The auditor also concedes the other two clauses: the build is awaited before the preview starts, and readiness does not parse printed URLs. So the stated reason does not defeat the pass.
